title: Sign in with a website access key
description: Use this guide when someone needs to sign in to the website with an access key instead of Google, or to revoke one.
content:
# Sign in with a website access key

A website access key lets someone sign into your Port OS account without using
your Google account. It grants full account access, including approval of AI
connections. Create one only for someone you trust. For plugin review, use a
dedicated account with sample devices and no access to your household.

## Create a key

1. Sign in to Port OS with Google.
2. Open Tokens and select Create access key.
3. Choose Website sign-in, enter a name, and choose an expiry of one hour, one
   day or seven days.
4. Create the key and copy it. Port OS shows it only once.

Keep the key private. Send reviewer credentials through the platform's private
reviewer-access fields, never a public package, chat message, repository or URL.

## Sign in and connect an assistant

On the sign-in screen, expand Sign in with an access key and paste the key.
Port OS checks its signature, expiry and active record before signing you in.
If you arrived from an assistant's OAuth connection, remain on that consent
screen and review the requested permissions before approving.

The plugin connects to the Port OS cloud. It needs no local MCP server.
Provider sign-in and MFA still happen through the provider-linking flow.

API and automation keys cannot sign into the website or approve connections.
Website keys cannot create replacement keys or be refreshed into a new session.
When a key expires, sign in again with Google to create a replacement.

## Revoke access

Revoke the key on Tokens. Its subsequent website and API requests will fail.
OAuth connections already approved with it are separate grants: revoke those
connections separately through the existing connection/grant controls. Deleting
a key does not disconnect an assistant that was already authorized.

## Troubleshooting

If the form rejects a key, check that it is a Website sign-in key and has not
expired or been revoked. Check network connectivity. Use Google sign-in to
recover account access and create a new key. Do not paste a provider API key,
refresh token or private signing key into the form.

If creation says website sign-in keys are unavailable, the cloud service may
still be updating. The website rejects incompatible API keys and attempts to
revoke them. If it asks you to revoke a remaining key, do so on Tokens before
retrying after the service update.

title: Add devices through provider linking
description: Use this guide when the customer wants to add devices by linking a provider account such as Google, Alexa or Tuya.
content:
# Add devices through provider linking

Read the public [plugin catalog](https://portoperatingsystem.com/plugins/). Match the provider by its exact name, then inspect supported capabilities, prerequisites, limitations and current availability before asking the user to sign in.

Devices enter Port OS through a plugin/provider account link. The user performs sign-in/consent on the provider and Port OS pages; an agent must not ask for their password. After linking, enumerate authorized endpoints and inspect actual capabilities. Catalog availability does not guarantee every vendor device implements every action.

Use [first setup](/docs/for-ai/guides/first-setup.md) to verify one safe device and [troubleshooting](/docs/for-ai/guides/troubleshooting.md) for expired provider links.

title: Authentication and dynamic client registration
description: Use this guide for the complete walkthrough from discovery to token refresh when you connect a new REST client.
content:
# Authentication and dynamic client registration

All supported agents use the same OAuth components. REST and MCP select different protected resources; DCR and CIMD select different registration methods. Neither product branding nor registration grants device access.

Choose one reading path. This complete walkthrough already includes discovery, registration, consent, token lifecycle and authorization rules below; you do not need to fetch those component links again. If your connector already implements some steps, read only the missing components instead. Both paths use the same canonical instructions.

For REST, use the discovered issuer as the OAuth resource. For MCP, use the MCP protected-resource metadata. Keep that choice through authorization, exchange and refresh. If you chose the wrong transport, start a new authorization flow for the correct resource; refresh does not switch audiences.

Walkthrough steps (the linked components are also included below):

1. [Discover endpoints and choose REST or MCP](/docs/for-ai/guides/oauth-discovery.md).
2. [Register with DCR or supported CIMD](/docs/for-ai/guides/oauth-client-registration.md). Remote callbacks require HTTPS; local callback registrations contain only localhost/loopback callbacks. Repeated canonical fingerprints reuse the original public client without expanding scopes.
3. [Obtain user consent and validate the callback](/docs/for-ai/guides/oauth-consent-and-callback.md). PKCE S256 is required. Pause for the user to sign in and approve access.
4. [Exchange, refresh and revoke tokens](/docs/for-ai/guides/oauth-token-lifecycle.md). Keep the same canonical resource through authorization, exchange and refresh.
5. [Verify the connection](/docs/for-ai/guides/first-setup.md), then use [the REST quickstart](/docs/for-ai/guides/quickstart.md) or your client's MCP tools.

Read [authorization rules](/docs/for-ai/guides/authorization-rules.md) for scopes, principal/resource policies, sharing and denial diagnosis. Never ask for a Google password, paste credentials into chat, or approve the agent's own grant. Claimed client names such as Muse and Grok remain unverified.

## Discover the OAuth server and choose REST or MCP

This discovery step is shared by every client. The API is https://api.portoperatingsystem.com and the authorization server is https://auth.portoperatingsystem.com. Fetch the API's /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server document anonymously. Read issuer, authorization_endpoint, token_endpoint, registration_endpoint, revocation_endpoint and scopes_supported. Use the returned auth endpoints exactly. The issuer and API resource have different origins; do not use the auth issuer as the API destination or token audience. Port OS exposes OAuth authorization-server metadata here; it does not advertise OpenID Connect discovery or issue OpenID Connect ID tokens.

| Interface | API destination | OAuth resource |
| --- | --- | --- |
| REST | https://api.portoperatingsystem.com plus the documented operation path | https://api.portoperatingsystem.com |
| MCP | https://api.portoperatingsystem.com/mcp, Streamable HTTP | The resource returned by /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp |

An MCP connector can start at https://api.portoperatingsystem.com/mcp and follow its WWW-Authenticate resource_metadata URL. Fetch that public metadata and the authorization server it names. MCP initialization alone does not prove that the account's devices are accessible. Never use a REST token on MCP or an MCP token on REST.

Choose the transport before authorizing. Omitting resource at authorization selects REST. Supply the discovered resource explicitly to select MCP. Code exchange and refresh may omit resource and inherit the grant audience; an explicit resource must stay unchanged. If a REST request fails because you authorized the MCP resource (or the reverse), obtain a new user authorization for the correct resource. Refresh cannot change the token's audience.

Choose one supported [client registration method](/docs/for-ai/guides/oauth-client-registration.md), then follow the same [consent and callback steps](/docs/for-ai/guides/oauth-consent-and-callback.md). If metadata omits registration_endpoint, new DCR registration is unavailable; do not guess a replacement endpoint or silently switch to another client's credentials.

See [scopes and resource rules](/docs/for-ai/guides/authorization-rules.md). Authorization-server scopes_supported describes server vocabulary; a particular client's accepted scopes can be narrower.

### Carry discovery values into every request

This JavaScript fragment initializes a REST connection. Keep `authorizationServer` and `resource` for the consent and token examples; the API base is the protected resource, independently of the discovered auth issuer.

```javascript
const apiBase = 'https://api.portoperatingsystem.com';
const response = await fetch(apiBase + '/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server');
if (!response.ok) throw new Error('OAuth discovery failed');
const authorizationServer = await response.json();
const resource = apiBase;
```

For MCP, assign `resource` from the protected-resource metadata's `resource` field instead. Keep the auth issuer separate from the API resource. A wrong `resource` can produce an `invalid_target` error callback even when client registration succeeded.

Canonical component: [Discover the OAuth server and choose REST or MCP](/docs/for-ai/guides/oauth-discovery.md).

## Register an OAuth client with DCR or CIMD

Start with [discovery](/docs/for-ai/guides/oauth-discovery.md). DCR and CIMD identify a client; they do not sign in a user or grant device access. Both use the same [PKCE consent and callback flow](/docs/for-ai/guides/oauth-consent-and-callback.md) and [token lifecycle](/docs/for-ai/guides/oauth-token-lifecycle.md).

### DCR: public clients

POST application/json to the discovered registration_endpoint:

```json
{"client_name":"My device assistant","redirect_uris":["https://your-client.example/oauth/callback"],"token_endpoint_auth_method":"none","grant_types":["authorization_code","refresh_token"],"response_types":["code"],"scope":"endpoint:read message:send"}
```

Use a callback the client controls. Remote callbacks require HTTPS. Local clients may use exact HTTP callbacks on localhost or literal loopback IPs, such as http://127.0.0.1:8765/callback. All callbacks in a registration must be local or all must be remote; these sets cannot be mixed. No fragments or user information are permitted. Start the local callback listener before authorization. The website's client-management interface enforces this same callback-set policy.

Success is 201 with client_id, client_id_issued_at and accepted metadata. Public clients get no client_secret. Supported DCR scopes are endpoint:read, endpoint:write, message:read, message:send, group:read, group:manage, subscription:read and subscription:write. The default is endpoint:read. Request only the task's necessary scopes and check the returned scope. Broader static-client scopes are outside this anonymous profile.

The registration fingerprint is SHA-256 of compact canonical JSON with sorted object keys and sorted redirect_uris, grant_types and response_types arrays, plus client_name and token_endpoint_auth_method. Defaults are applied before hashing. Array ordering does not create another client. A matching registration returns the original client ID, issue time, scopes and descriptive metadata. It never overwrites the existing client or expands scopes, even if scope or software_id differs in the new request. Fingerprinting is deduplication, not proof of callback ownership or vendor identity.

Default quotas are 1,000 new registrations per rolling day and 10,000 retained registrations. Reuse does not consume new-registration quota. A quota failure returns 429 with Retry-After. An operator can disable new registrations without retiring existing grants. Read the [registration operation](/docs/for-ai/operations/registerDynamicOAuthClient.md) for exact request, response and error schemas.

### CIMD: metadata clients

A CIMD client uses its HTTPS metadata URL as client_id instead of posting a DCR request. Any HTTPS metadata URL is accepted. Port OS retrieves and validates that client metadata on every authorization attempt, including its exact HTTPS callbacks and public PKCE profile. Loopback, private and link-local metadata hosts and redirects from the metadata fetch are refused. Do not pretend another client's metadata URL belongs to you.

Client_name, software_id, software_version and client_uri remain unverified claims. No trusted software-statement issuer is configured; software_statement is rejected. A registration called Muse or Grok does not establish a verified vendor integration or gain additional permissions. Static confidential clients retain their separately configured client authentication method.

Canonical component: [Register an OAuth client with DCR or CIMD](/docs/for-ai/guides/oauth-client-registration.md).

## Obtain user consent and validate the OAuth callback

Use the endpoints and resource from [discovery](/docs/for-ai/guides/oauth-discovery.md) and the client ID and exact callback from [registration](/docs/for-ai/guides/oauth-client-registration.md). These steps are identical for DCR and CIMD, REST and MCP; the chosen resource is the transport-specific input.

`resource` is optional. Omitting it selects the canonical REST audience (the authorization-server issuer). For MCP, supply its discovered `/mcp` resource explicitly. Token exchange and refresh can omit `resource` and inherit the audience bound to the authorization code or refresh token. Explicit mismatches are rejected as `invalid_target`.

1. Start the callback handler the client controls. For a loopback callback, bind its listener locally before opening authorization.
2. Generate a cryptographically random PKCE verifier of 43–128 permitted characters. Compute code_challenge = BASE64URL(SHA256(verifier)), without padding. Generate a separate random state and retain both in this authorization attempt.
3. Open the discovered authorization_endpoint with the following query parameters. Percent-encode parameter values; do not append raw callback URLs or scopes into an unescaped query.

```text
client_id=<registered ID or supported CIMD metadata URL>
redirect_uri=<exact registered callback>
response_type=code
scope=<requested subset of the client's accepted scopes>
resource=<chosen canonical REST or MCP resource>
state=<random client state>
code_challenge=<S256 challenge>
code_challenge_method=S256
```

For REST, use the `resource = authorizationServer.issuer` value retained from discovery. Construct the URL rather than writing an alias into a template. This JavaScript fragment assumes `clientId`, `redirectUri` and `acceptedScope` come from your registration response and callback configuration:

```javascript
const base64url = bytes => btoa(String.fromCharCode(...bytes))
  .replaceAll('+', '-').replaceAll('/', '_').replace(/=+$/, '');
const verifier = base64url(crypto.getRandomValues(new Uint8Array(32)));
const state = base64url(crypto.getRandomValues(new Uint8Array(32)));
const challenge = base64url(new Uint8Array(await crypto.subtle.digest(
  'SHA-256', new TextEncoder().encode(verifier))));
const authorizationURL = new URL(authorizationServer.authorization_endpoint);
authorizationURL.search = new URLSearchParams({
  client_id: clientId, redirect_uri: redirectUri, response_type: 'code',
  scope: acceptedScope, resource, state,
  code_challenge: challenge, code_challenge_method: 'S256',
}).toString();
// Retain verifier, state and authorizationServer.issuer privately until callback validation.
// Open authorizationURL.href in the user's browser; wait for their consent.
```

The user signs in on Port OS and reviews the requested permissions. Pause for the user; an agent must not approve its own grant, request passwords or manufacture a production sign-in identity. Local functional tests substitute an existing signed fixture identity at this boundary without changing production sign-in.

After approval, the consent page navigates to a one-time Port OS continuation.
That endpoint returns HTTP 302 Found with the exact registered callback in
Location, carrying code, original state and iss. Denial uses the same 302 handoff
with access_denied instead of a code. The authenticated consent fetch returns
200 JSON only for the intermediate continuation; it must be followed by document
navigation, not another fetch. Continuations expire after two minutes and are
single-use. They require no login token and cannot be used to approve consent.

Reject a callback whose state or issuer does not match this attempt. Treat an
error callback as a denied or failed authorization, not a code. Codes and pending
consent expire after ten minutes and are single-use. Do not paste codes,
continuation references or credentials into shared chat or logs. Continue with
[code exchange and token lifecycle](/docs/for-ai/guides/oauth-token-lifecycle.md).

For hosted-client acceptance, preserve the browser network log and approve a
fresh request. Verify the document request to /oauth/authorization-response
returns 302, the next GET reaches the registered client callback, and the client
posts its code and original PKCE verifier to the discovered token endpoint.
Repeat with Deny and verify access_denied without a code. Backend functional and
website browser tests cover these boundaries against an isolated callback;
compatibility with a specific hosted client still requires that live trace.

Canonical component: [Obtain user consent and validate the OAuth callback](/docs/for-ai/guides/oauth-consent-and-callback.md).

## Exchange, refresh and revoke scoped OAuth tokens

Complete [callback validation](/docs/for-ai/guides/oauth-consent-and-callback.md) first. For a public DCR/CIMD client, POST application/x-www-form-urlencoded to the discovered token_endpoint with:

```text
grant_type=authorization_code
client_id=<client ID used for authorization>
code=<validated callback code>
redirect_uri=<the same exact callback>
code_verifier=<this attempt's original verifier>
resource=<the same canonical resource used for authorization>
```

Continue with the same discovery values and verifier from the consent example. `code` below must be from a callback whose `state` and `iss` you validated; abort on any callback `error`:

```javascript
const tokenResponse = await fetch(authorizationServer.token_endpoint, {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded' },
  body: new URLSearchParams({
    grant_type: 'authorization_code', client_id: clientId, code,
    redirect_uri: redirectUri, code_verifier: verifier, resource,
  }),
});
if (!tokenResponse.ok) throw new Error('OAuth code exchange failed');
const tokens = await tokenResponse.json(); // Store securely; do not print tokens.
```

Save access_token, refresh_token and returned scope in the connector's secure credential store. Public clients have no client secret. Use Authorization: Bearer <access_token> with REST requests or the MCP HTTP connection, according to that token's resource. A refresh token is never an API credential. [Scopes bound access; resource policies still apply](/docs/for-ai/guides/authorization-rules.md).

Refresh with grant_type=refresh_token, client_id and refresh_token at token_endpoint. The resource parameter is optional for code exchange and refresh: omission inherits the existing grant audience; if supplied, it must match the original resource. Scope may stay the same or narrow; it cannot expand. Credentials rotate: store the newly returned refresh token atomically and stop using the previous one. A revoked or reused refresh token must not be retried in a loop. Reauthorize when the grant no longer permits the intended operation.

Revoke by POSTing application/x-www-form-urlencoded token=<refresh_token>&client_id=<client_id> to revocation_endpoint. Revoked grants stop authorizing both access and refresh requests. Removing a local configuration file alone is not server-side revocation.

Read [the token operation](/docs/for-ai/operations/generateToken.md), [revocation operation](/docs/for-ai/operations/revokeOAuthGrant.md), and [connection recovery](/docs/for-ai/guides/troubleshooting.md) for schemas and failures. Verify account access using [first setup](/docs/for-ai/guides/first-setup.md), then perform only the customer's intended task. Dispatch acceptance is distinct from observed device state.

Canonical component: [Exchange, refresh and revoke scoped OAuth tokens](/docs/for-ai/guides/oauth-token-lifecycle.md).

## Set up access rules for Port OS

Authentication establishes the principal and client. OAuth scopes bound the user's delegated authority; resource rules decide which selected resources and actions that principal may access. A scope is not an ownership or sharing grant.

For delegated REST grants, Port OS verifies token signature, expiry, issuer, REST audience, access-token type and active grant, then checks the operation's scope before existing service resource-policy evaluation. MCP tokens have a separate /mcp audience and cannot be reused on REST. A refresh token is never an API bearer credential.

| Task | Scope |
| --- | --- |
| Enumerate or query endpoints/routes | endpoint:read |
| Modify endpoints/routes | endpoint:write |
| Send a device message | message:send |
| Read groups and relationships | group:read |
| Manage group membership | group:manage |
| Read subscriptions | subscription:read |
| Create/update/delete subscriptions | subscription:write |

MCP uses the same scopes as the REST operation that does the same work. Listing, inspecting or discovering subscribable events (`subscription_list`, `subscription_inspect`, `events/list`) needs subscription:read. Subscribing, unsubscribing, cancelling or relabelling (`events/subscribe`, `events/unsubscribe`, `subscription_cancel`, `subscription_label_edit`) needs subscription:write. Subscribing to a device's events does not need endpoint:read; whether the principal may see the source endpoint is a resource rule. Task guides and capability reference documents need only a valid MCP token. A call without the needed scope gets 403 `insufficient_scope` naming the scope to request. An MCP connection approved before these scopes existed must be re-approved to get them; its existing event deliveries continue.

Other operations are outside the anonymous DCR device profile and fail closed. [Operation pages](/docs/for-ai/operations/index.md) expose exact credential alternatives and resource requirements. [Machine-readable authorization metadata](/docs/references/authorization.yaml) links the contract.

The existing resource engine converts principal, action, resource and entity data into Cedar requests. Default owner rules and applicable sharing/conditional rules are evaluated; only an Allow outcome admits access. The typed operation IDs come from Port OS's policy action catalog, not invented dotted action names. Owning an endpoint does not override a delegated token's missing scope.

A token with endpoint:read can enumerate permitted lights but cannot dispatch a command. Adding message:send permits dispatch only to endpoints that the signed-in principal's rules allow. An authorized light does not imply camera access. A generic power-capable plug is not automatically a light. For a group request, evaluate the selected targets and report denied or unresolved members separately.

An invalid/expired/revoked token needs renewed authentication. A scope denial requires the user to approve the needed scope. A resource denial requires the owner to grant the appropriate resource/action access. Never fix denial by switching principal, requesting unrestricted credentials or retrying blindly. Provider authentication failures can require account relinking; they are different from Port OS policy denial. Keep inaccessible resource identities out of diagnostics.

See [troubleshooting](/docs/for-ai/guides/troubleshooting.md).

Canonical component: [Set up access rules for Port OS](/docs/for-ai/guides/authorization-rules.md).

title: Read camera captures and streams
description: Use this guide when the customer wants a camera snapshot, a recording or a live stream.
content:
# Read camera captures and streams

Camera access requires both the operation scope and authorization for the selected camera/action. A light-control grant does not imply imagery access. Discover camera/snapshot capabilities from [the directory](/docs/for-ai/capability-interfaces.md) and use only declared message schemas.

Prefer an on-demand capture when the user asks for a current image. Validate the returned media URI, timeOfSample and URI expiry. An existing capture may be old even when its download URI is new. Confirm the media is actually retrievable before describing it as viewed. If expired or stale, request a new permitted capture or explain the limitation. Streams require the declared lifecycle/transport, not an invented snapshot API.

Read [authorization rules](/docs/for-ai/guides/authorization-rules.md) and [async outcomes](/docs/for-ai/guides/using-the-api.md).

title: Connect any supported agent to Port OS
description: Use this guide to connect a supported AI agent to Port OS and to copy the setup prompt.
content:
# Connect any supported agent to Port OS

Use these common components for Muse, Grok, Claude, a custom REST agent or an MCP connector. The product name does not change the authorization protocol or permissions. Check your client's current capabilities before assuming it supports a particular registration method.

For a new REST connection, read the [complete authentication walkthrough](/docs/for-ai/guides/authentication-and-dcr.md), then the [REST quickstart](/docs/for-ai/guides/quickstart.md). The walkthrough includes the OAuth components in the table below; you can skip their separate files. For an existing connector, use the table to read only the component you need. This directory is a set of alternatives, not a checklist of required downloads.

Copy this prompt into a client that can retrieve public documents:

> Read https://portoperatingsystem.com/docs/for-ai/guides/connect-agent.md. Discover Port OS authentication, choose REST or MCP and a registration method supported by this client, and help me connect. Pause for me to sign in and approve the requested access, then list only devices I can access. Do not claim device control until its result is observed.

| Component | Input | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [Discovery and transport](/docs/for-ai/guides/oauth-discovery.md) | Public API/MCP URL | The sign-in server address, its endpoints, and the REST and MCP resource URLs |
| [DCR or CIMD registration](/docs/for-ai/guides/oauth-client-registration.md) | Client-supported method and controlled callback | Client identity and accepted profile, without device access |
| [User consent and callback](/docs/for-ai/guides/oauth-consent-and-callback.md) | Client ID, callback, resource and least scopes | Validated one-use authorization code |
| [Token lifecycle](/docs/for-ai/guides/oauth-token-lifecycle.md) | Code and original PKCE verifier | Scoped access, refresh rotation and revocation |
| [Authorization rules](/docs/for-ai/guides/authorization-rules.md) | Token scopes and customer's permissions | Effective authority and an explanation of denials |
| [First setup](/docs/for-ai/guides/first-setup.md) | Authorized connection | Device discovery and one safe verification |

An MCP-capable client normally manages OAuth and secure token storage itself; supply the MCP URL and complete its consent flow. A REST agent needs an execution environment with HTTP requests, a real callback listener, cryptographic random generation and secure token storage. If the client cannot receive a callback or securely retain credentials, explain the missing capability instead of inventing a bypass.

Client-specific screens can provide UI settings or support notes and link to this table. They must not maintain their own copies of DCR, PKCE, scope, callback or revocation instructions. Actual client/version compatibility and vendor identity require separate validation; the shared guide makes no verified Muse/Grok claim.
setupPrompt: Read https://portoperatingsystem.com/docs/for-ai/guides/connect-agent.md. Discover Port OS authentication, choose REST or MCP and a registration method supported by this client, and help me connect. Pause for me to sign in and approve the requested access, then list only devices I can access. Do not claim device control until its result is observed.

title: Grant permissions to endpoints
description: Use this guide when the customer wants to decide who or what may read or control a device.
content:
# Grant permissions to endpoints

Give a user or agent access to a selected device. You must own the endpoint or have permission to manage its access.

## Choose the resource and principal

1. Open [Your Devices](https://portoperatingsystem.com/dashboard/) and select the endpoint.
2. Copy its full endpoint ID. Device names can repeat.
3. Identify the principal that needs access. A principal is the user or agent identity that Port OS checks when it receives a request.

## Grant the required actions

Read the existing rules with [Get access control rules](/docs/for-ai/operations/getAccessControlRules.md). Use [Upsert an access control rule](/docs/for-ai/operations/upsertAccessControlRule.md) to grant the selected principal only the actions it needs on the full endpoint ID. Follow the operation's policy schema and action identifiers; do not use a display name as a resource ID. For example, allow endpoint discovery for reading, and message sending for control. See [Access rules](/docs/for-ai/guides/authorization-rules.md) for policy evaluation and required OAuth scopes.

## Check and remove access

Test with the receiving account or agent. Confirm it can use the intended endpoint. Remove the grant when access is no longer needed.

A scope error requires a new OAuth approval with the required scope. A resource denial requires the owner to change the resource grant. Adding a scope alone does not share a device.

title: Send commands to an endpoint and read its events
description: Use this guide to understand events, capabilities and messages, and how a device state change reaches you.
content:
# How to send commands to an endpoint and read its events

Find out what an endpoint can do, send it a supported command, and read what it reports back. You will use the same messages to control an endpoint and to learn when something happens to it.

## Messages

To control an endpoint, or to learn when something has happened to it, you handle messages.

You send a message to an endpoint to control it. You receive a message from an endpoint to learn what it observed or did.

## Capabilities

An endpoint tells you what it can do by declaring capabilities.

A capability defines a set of messages that an endpoint can send or receive.

A capability namespace such as `port1/systems/zero/capability-interfaces/power` tells you that the endpoint can support power controls. Read the [capability reference](https://portoperatingsystem.com/docs/reference/capabilities/) for the messages each capability defines.

To find out which messages an endpoint supports, look at the capabilities it declares. See the [API reference](https://portoperatingsystem.com/api/) for how to list an endpoint and its capabilities.

An endpoint can declare a subset of a capability's messages. A declared subset limits which commands are available, so do not assume that every message in a capability works on every endpoint. An omitted subset uses the versioned capability contract. An explicitly empty subset advertises no messages.

## Send a message

A message has a header identifying its capability namespace and message name, and a body that follows the message schema. For an endpoint that advertises power `turn-on`, the payload is:

```json
{
  "header": {
    "namespace": "port1/systems/zero/capability-interfaces/power",
    "name": "turn-on"
  },
  "body": {}
}
```

Use the [send-message operation](/docs/for-ai/operations/sendMessage.md) for the enclosing request and target format. Choose the full endpoint ID returned by discovery. Dispatch only a supported message to an endpoint you intend to operate.

## Read attributes and events

Attributes describe observations, such as the power capability's `power` attribute with a value of `ON` or `OFF`. They differ from command messages: accepting `turn-on` does not prove that the endpoint is on. Read the endpoint's reported attributes after dispatch when the connection supports observation.

Events communicate changes through the event transport supported by your client. An incoming command asks an endpoint to act; an outgoing capability message reports an event. Match namespace, version, name and schema when interpreting an event. See [MCP setup](/docs/for-ai/guides/connect-agent.md) and [the API guide](/docs/for-ai/guides/using-the-api.md) for client and transport details.

When a current power observation is unavailable, offer explicit On and Off commands that the endpoint supports rather than inventing a current state. This also applies when a connection normally reports state but a read fails. When power is known, use that observation for the toggle. Keep pending actions, command acceptance and confirmed observations separate; an accepted command with missing readback remains unconfirmed.

## Recover from missing data or failures

An empty attribute list does not mean the endpoint is off. A failed read leaves the state unknown. A timeout may follow a successful physical action: check observations before repeating a command, especially relative actions. For a permission error, check both OAuth scopes and the resource grant in [authorization rules](/docs/for-ai/guides/authorization-rules.md). If a command is absent, choose one the endpoint advertises or reconnect the provider when discovery is out of date.

title: First setup and connection verification
description: Use this guide the first time a customer connects Port OS, to set up access and verify the connection end to end.
content:
# First setup and connection verification

Use [the quickstart](/docs/for-ai/guides/quickstart.md). Check three stages separately: reachable metadata/API, a valid authenticated token, and access to the intended resources. A protocol connection alone is not device access.

Enumerate first. An empty account may need [provider linking](/docs/for-ai/guides/adding-devices.md) or a sharing grant. Select one safe test light and explain the intended command. Follow its exact schema. Read fresh state afterward; ask the user to confirm physically when no reliable observation exists. Record no passwords or tokens in conversation.

If authorization expires, refresh within the original grant or ask the user to authorize again. Confirm grant revocation in account settings or the documented revocation endpoint. See [troubleshooting](/docs/for-ai/guides/troubleshooting.md).

title: Connect Google Nest
description: Use this guide when the customer wants to link Google Nest to read thermostats and temperature sensors, or to view cameras.
content:
# Connect Google Nest

Link Google Nest to Port OS to read and control thermostats and to view cameras. You can link it two ways:

- **Your own Google Cloud client** (`customer-oauth`): you create a Google Cloud OAuth client and a Device Access project, and give Port OS the client ID, the client secret and the Device Access project ID. Available to any account. Live events are not available on this variant.
- **Port OS's client** (`portos-oauth`): Port OS uses its own OAuth client and Device Access project. This is available only to accounts that Port OS has granted access, and it includes live events.

The website flow saves first, then authorizes: you save your values as a draft connection, then choose Authorize. Nothing is connected until Google returns and Port OS completes the link.

## Your own Google Cloud client [#customer-oauth]

1. In the [Google Cloud console](https://console.cloud.google.com), create or select a project, then open APIs and Services, Credentials.
   <!-- screenshot: nest-gcp-credentials -->
2. Choose Create credentials, OAuth client ID, and set the application type to Web application.
   <!-- screenshot: nest-gcp-create-oauth-client -->
3. In Port OS, open the Google Nest connect screen and choose the option to use your own Google Cloud client. Copy the Redirect URI it shows.
   <!-- screenshot: nest-portos-connect-redirect -->
4. Paste that value into the OAuth client's Authorized redirect URIs and save. It must exactly match the value the connect screen shows.
   <!-- screenshot: nest-gcp-redirect-uri -->
5. Copy the OAuth client ID and client secret.
   <!-- screenshot: nest-gcp-client-credentials -->
6. In the [Device Access console](https://console.nest.google.com/device-access), create a project. Google charges a one-time US$5 registration fee for Device Access; see Google's Device Access console for current terms. When asked for an OAuth client ID, enter the client ID from step 5, which links the OAuth client to the project.
   <!-- screenshot: nest-device-access-create-project -->
7. Copy the Device Access project ID from the project page.
   <!-- screenshot: nest-device-access-project-id -->
8. In Port OS, paste the client ID, the client secret and the Device Access project ID, and choose Save. This creates a draft; the secret is stored on the backend and never shown again.
   <!-- screenshot: nest-portos-save-credentials -->
9. Choose Authorize. Google asks you to approve access to your Nest devices; approve it. Port OS then lists your devices and shows Nest as connected.
   <!-- screenshot: nest-consent -->

### What works on this variant

- Only thermostat reads and control work. Temperature sensors, motion, doorbell, camera event images and camera live video need Port OS's own client, so they are not available on this connection.
- No Pub/Sub topic or subscription is needed. Live events (motion, doorbell, camera event images and pushed temperature changes) are not available; Port OS shows events as unsupported for this connection rather than as an error. Read current state instead.
- Changing the OAuth client ID or the Device Access project ID requires deleting the connection and connecting again.

### Redirect URI

The Authorized redirect URI in Google Cloud must match the value the Port OS connect screen shows, character for character, including the scheme, host, path and any trailing slash. Google sends you back to the Port OS auth host, which relays the result to the website.

## Use Port OS's client [#portos-oauth]

If your account has been granted Port OS's Nest client, the connect screen offers a Port OS client option. You do not create a Google Cloud client or a Device Access project. Live events are included.

1. Open the Google Nest connect screen and choose the Port OS client option.
   <!-- screenshot: nest-portos-oauth-choice -->
2. Choose Authorize and approve the requested access on Google.
   <!-- screenshot: nest-portos-oauth-consent -->

If the option is missing, your account has not been granted access. Use your own Google Cloud client instead.

## Troubleshooting

- **Redirect mismatch (Google shows "redirect_uri_mismatch").** The Authorized redirect URI differs from the one Port OS shows. Copy it again from the connect screen and save the OAuth client in Google Cloud.
- **Invalid client (`invalid_client`).** The client ID or secret is wrong, or the secret was replaced. Re-enter both and save again before authorizing.
- **The device list fails after you approve.** The Device Access project ID is wrong, or the OAuth client is not linked to that project. Port OS requests the device list when it completes the link, so a wrong project ID fails the connection. Check the project ID and the linked client ID in the Device Access console, then delete the connection and connect again. An account with no devices connects with an empty list; that is not an error.
- **`AUTH_LINK_NOT_READY`.** The connection is still a draft that is missing required values: the client ID, the client secret or the Device Access project ID. Save all three, then authorize.
- **Stale callback.** An authorization that was started earlier, or opened twice, can return after it expired or was replaced. Close the tab and choose Authorize again. Changing the Device Access project or client ID on an existing connection means deleting the connection and connecting again; the previous attempt is not reused.

title: How to turn off your lights
description: Use this guide to turn lights off or on, or to check whether lights are on. It covers finding the right lights, telling lights from switches and plugs, and fixing device data that causes confusion.
content:
# How to turn off your lights

1. Find your lights by listing your devices.
2. Check each device's capabilities and type.
3. Turn them off.

## Before you start: what does "all lights" mean?

"All lights", "the lights" and "lights" depend on your habits. Common meanings:

1. Turn off every light you own.
2. Turn off the lights in the room you are in.
3. Turn off every light in a group you named "all lights".
4. Turn off every light, switch and plug in one group, such as the main house, and leave the other groups alone.

Decide which of these you mean, and use the same meaning each time. If you are unsure, start with every endpoint of the `LIGHT` type. That is not always right, because some lamps are plugged into a switch or plug instead.

## Lights, switches and plugs

Start with authorized endpoint discovery and inspect each endpoint's capability declarations. A room name can be ambiguous, so select by full ID and group path, or name the room yourself. A plug or switch that supports power is not automatically a light.

Sometimes "turn off the lights" means turning off a plug or switch that a lamp is connected to. When you search for an endpoint, check plugs and switches as well as lights, and check that it is the lamp you mean before you switch it off.

## Lights in someone else's home

The lights may belong to someone else who shared them with you, for example when you are house sitting or staying in a rented home. Shared endpoints are not included by default. Add an explicit owner, endpoint ID or group selector to include them.

## Fix confusing data

Fix the data so that your devices are easy to recognize. For example, change a plug that powers a lamp to the `LIGHT` type. If a device does not work, disable it so that it stops appearing in default results.

## Use MCP

Connect your AI client with the steps in [How to use MCP](https://portoperatingsystem.com/docs/how-to-use-mcp/). Then ask your assistant to do the work, or call these tools directly:

- `endpoint_query` lists devices. It returns each device's type, capabilities and message IDs. Call it without a `query` to load everything, or narrow it with a type filter such as `{"type": {"eq": "LIGHT"}}`. Pass the returned `nextToken` back until none is returned. Ask for `expand: ["power"]` to read power state, and add `forceDeviceAttributeQuery: true` to read it from the device instead of the cache.
- `group_query` lists groups, their parent path, child groups and members. Use it to resolve a room to a full group ID.
- `control` sends a command. Copy `id` and `message` from the query results, for example the `turn-off` message of the power capability, and send `payload: {}`.
- `endpoint_manage` repairs data. Its operations are `RENAME`, `SET_TYPE`, `SET_ENABLEMENT`, `MERGE_INTO` and `DELETE`. Copy the full endpoint ID from `endpoint_query`, and understand the effect before you merge or delete.
- `group_manage` creates, renames, merges and deletes groups, and changes their members.

Check the results to see which lights were selected, which commands were accepted, and which failed.

## Use the HTTP API

Authorize with a bearer token that has the endpoint and message permissions you need. See [authorization rules](/docs/for-ai/guides/authorization-rules.md).

### Find lights

For one bulb, read its power, brightness and color message schemas in [the capability directory](/docs/for-ai/capability-interfaces.md). Use the exact namespace, version, message name, units and constraints it returns. [The quickstart](/docs/for-ai/guides/quickstart.md) shows the generic message envelope.

For "all lights", call [endpointQuery](/docs/for-ai/operations/endpointQuery.md) with `endpoint:read` permission and filter by the `LIGHT` type:

```json
{
  "query": {
    "match": {"key": "type", "value": "LIGHT"}
  },
  "paginationContext": {"maxResults": 25}
}
```

Type-only queries return the caller's own endpoints. To include a shared endpoint, add an explicit owner or endpoint ID selector. A group selector can include shared members once `group:read` and group access checks pass.

For a room, first resolve its full group ID with [group discovery](/docs/for-ai/guides/managing-groups.md). Then add `{"match":{"key":"groupId","value":"<resolved-full-group-id>"}}` to the `and` list of the query. This also requires `group:read` and permission to read that group. A group filter returns the group's member endpoints. Resolve nested groups as needed and remove duplicate endpoint IDs. Reading a group does not grant control of its members.

Repeat the same query, page size and authenticated grant with `paginationContext.nextToken` from each response. Continue until the token is absent, including after an empty page. Disabled endpoints are excluded by default. Check each selected endpoint's declared capabilities, and drop targets that do not support power. Do not widen the selection to every plug or switch. Freeze the target list before you send commands, and report each result.

### Read state

To read live state, call [endpointQuery](/docs/for-ai/operations/endpointQuery.md) with `expand: ["interfaces.attributes"]` and `forceDeviceQuery: true`. The same options exist on `GET /endpoints`: send `id=<endpoint-id>`, `expand=interfaces.attributes` and `forceDeviceAttributeQuery=true`. Check each observation's sample time and any partial errors before you say a light changed.

A batch can partly succeed. Report selected, accepted, failed and unresolved targets separately. A lost response is not a reason to repeat a relative brightness change.

### Control lights

Send each command with [sendMessage](/docs/for-ai/operations/sendMessage.md): `POST /messages` with the target endpoint and a message that names the capability namespace, message name and version. To turn a light off:

```json
{
  "target": {
    "type": "ENDPOINT",
    "id": "<full-endpoint-id-from-discovery>"
  },
  "message": {
    "header": {
      "namespace": "port1/systems/zero/capability-interfaces/power",
      "name": "turn-off",
      "version": "1.0"
    },
    "body": {}
  }
}
```

An accepted command does not prove the light is off. Read the state again to confirm.

title: Manage device names and availability
description: Use this guide when the customer wants to rename a device, change its availability or find it by name.
content:
# Manage device names and availability

Select the exact endpoint and read [its management operation](/docs/for-ai/operations/index.md). Rename, enable/disable, delete or synchronize only where the published operation and device/provider support it. Use endpoint:write plus the required resource rule; control scope alone is insufficient.

Do not disable or delete a device merely because it is confusing or unavailable. Explain the effect and follow the user's intent. Apply documented ETag/version preconditions, inspect conflicts and preserve newer edits. If a response says the edit committed with cleanup pending, read back state before retrying. See [groups](/docs/for-ai/guides/managing-groups.md) and [troubleshooting](/docs/for-ai/guides/troubleshooting.md).

title: Manage groups and membership
description: Use this guide when the customer wants to create a group, change its members or control devices by group.
content:
# Manage groups and membership

Use [group operation references](/docs/for-ai/operations/index.md), group:read for discovery and group:manage plus resource policy for changes. Copy full IDs. Names are labels and may not be unique.

Inspect nested membership, preserve relationship meaning and deduplicate targets. Rename, merge, add/remove members only through declared operations. Use documented idempotency and ETags/version checks. On concurrent edits, retrieve current state and resolve the conflict rather than overwrite it. Native media groups and spatial cleaning targets are different concepts; see [vacuum guidance](/docs/for-ai/guides/vacuums.md).

title: Manage simulator devices
description: Use this guide when the customer wants to create a simulator device to test a capability without real hardware.
content:
# Manage simulator devices

Test device control without physical hardware. Sign in to Port OS before you start.

## Create a simulator

1. Open [Simulators](https://portoperatingsystem.com/simulators/).
2. Select **New Simulator**.
3. Choose a light and give it a clear name.
4. Create it, then open its linked endpoint from [Your Devices](https://portoperatingsystem.com/dashboard/).

## Control the device

Use the endpoint power control to turn the light on or off. Read its returned power value to check the result. You can also use the simulator endpoint in the [Quick start](https://portoperatingsystem.com/docs/getting-started/) or connect an [AI client](https://portoperatingsystem.com/connect-ai/).

## Edit or remove a simulator

Open the simulator from the list. Use its edit or delete control. Removing a simulator removes your test device; confirm the selected device before deleting it.

If a simulator does not appear, refresh the list and confirm you are signed in to the same account. If a command fails, check endpoint permissions and try again after the pending command completes.

title: Control media playback
description: Use this guide when the customer wants to play, pause or search audio, set the volume or launch content on a media device.
content:
# Control media playback

Enumerate permitted media endpoints and inspect declared playback, volume and content-launcher capabilities in [the capability directory](/docs/for-ai/capability-interfaces.md). Select endpoint or native media group only when its declarations support the requested operation. Use [REST dispatch](/docs/for-ai/guides/quickstart.md) with the exact message/payload/version.

Absolute volume and relative volume changes have different retry behavior. Validate units/ranges. After dispatch, query fresh playback/volume observations. Accepted playback is not proof of audible output. On lost relative-command responses, recover the result/read back or report unknown; do not apply the increment twice.

title: Register an OAuth client with DCR or CIMD
description: Use this guide to register a public OAuth client with dynamic client registration or a client ID metadata document.
content:
# Register an OAuth client with DCR or CIMD

Start with [discovery](/docs/for-ai/guides/oauth-discovery.md). DCR and CIMD identify a client; they do not sign in a user or grant device access. Both use the same [PKCE consent and callback flow](/docs/for-ai/guides/oauth-consent-and-callback.md) and [token lifecycle](/docs/for-ai/guides/oauth-token-lifecycle.md).

## DCR: public clients

POST application/json to the discovered registration_endpoint:

```json
{"client_name":"My device assistant","redirect_uris":["https://your-client.example/oauth/callback"],"token_endpoint_auth_method":"none","grant_types":["authorization_code","refresh_token"],"response_types":["code"],"scope":"endpoint:read message:send"}
```

Use a callback the client controls. Remote callbacks require HTTPS. Local clients may use exact HTTP callbacks on localhost or literal loopback IPs, such as http://127.0.0.1:8765/callback. All callbacks in a registration must be local or all must be remote; these sets cannot be mixed. No fragments or user information are permitted. Start the local callback listener before authorization. The website's client-management interface enforces this same callback-set policy.

Success is 201 with client_id, client_id_issued_at and accepted metadata. Public clients get no client_secret. Supported DCR scopes are endpoint:read, endpoint:write, message:read, message:send, group:read, group:manage, subscription:read and subscription:write. The default is endpoint:read. Request only the task's necessary scopes and check the returned scope. Broader static-client scopes are outside this anonymous profile.

The registration fingerprint is SHA-256 of compact canonical JSON with sorted object keys and sorted redirect_uris, grant_types and response_types arrays, plus client_name and token_endpoint_auth_method. Defaults are applied before hashing. Array ordering does not create another client. A matching registration returns the original client ID, issue time, scopes and descriptive metadata. It never overwrites the existing client or expands scopes, even if scope or software_id differs in the new request. Fingerprinting is deduplication, not proof of callback ownership or vendor identity.

Default quotas are 1,000 new registrations per rolling day and 10,000 retained registrations. Reuse does not consume new-registration quota. A quota failure returns 429 with Retry-After. An operator can disable new registrations without retiring existing grants. Read the [registration operation](/docs/for-ai/operations/registerDynamicOAuthClient.md) for exact request, response and error schemas.

## CIMD: metadata clients

A CIMD client uses its HTTPS metadata URL as client_id instead of posting a DCR request. Any HTTPS metadata URL is accepted. Port OS retrieves and validates that client metadata on every authorization attempt, including its exact HTTPS callbacks and public PKCE profile. Loopback, private and link-local metadata hosts and redirects from the metadata fetch are refused. Do not pretend another client's metadata URL belongs to you.

Client_name, software_id, software_version and client_uri remain unverified claims. No trusted software-statement issuer is configured; software_statement is rejected. A registration called Muse or Grok does not establish a verified vendor integration or gain additional permissions. Static confidential clients retain their separately configured client authentication method.

title: Obtain user consent and validate the OAuth callback
description: Use this guide to send the customer to consent and to validate the callback before exchanging the code.
content:
# Obtain user consent and validate the OAuth callback

Use the endpoints and resource from [discovery](/docs/for-ai/guides/oauth-discovery.md) and the client ID and exact callback from [registration](/docs/for-ai/guides/oauth-client-registration.md). These steps are identical for DCR and CIMD, REST and MCP; the chosen resource is the transport-specific input.

`resource` is optional. Omitting it selects the canonical REST audience (the authorization-server issuer). For MCP, supply its discovered `/mcp` resource explicitly. Token exchange and refresh can omit `resource` and inherit the audience bound to the authorization code or refresh token. Explicit mismatches are rejected as `invalid_target`.

1. Start the callback handler the client controls. For a loopback callback, bind its listener locally before opening authorization.
2. Generate a cryptographically random PKCE verifier of 43–128 permitted characters. Compute code_challenge = BASE64URL(SHA256(verifier)), without padding. Generate a separate random state and retain both in this authorization attempt.
3. Open the discovered authorization_endpoint with the following query parameters. Percent-encode parameter values; do not append raw callback URLs or scopes into an unescaped query.

```text
client_id=<registered ID or supported CIMD metadata URL>
redirect_uri=<exact registered callback>
response_type=code
scope=<requested subset of the client's accepted scopes>
resource=<chosen canonical REST or MCP resource>
state=<random client state>
code_challenge=<S256 challenge>
code_challenge_method=S256
```

For REST, use the `resource = authorizationServer.issuer` value retained from discovery. Construct the URL rather than writing an alias into a template. This JavaScript fragment assumes `clientId`, `redirectUri` and `acceptedScope` come from your registration response and callback configuration:

```javascript
const base64url = bytes => btoa(String.fromCharCode(...bytes))
  .replaceAll('+', '-').replaceAll('/', '_').replace(/=+$/, '');
const verifier = base64url(crypto.getRandomValues(new Uint8Array(32)));
const state = base64url(crypto.getRandomValues(new Uint8Array(32)));
const challenge = base64url(new Uint8Array(await crypto.subtle.digest(
  'SHA-256', new TextEncoder().encode(verifier))));
const authorizationURL = new URL(authorizationServer.authorization_endpoint);
authorizationURL.search = new URLSearchParams({
  client_id: clientId, redirect_uri: redirectUri, response_type: 'code',
  scope: acceptedScope, resource, state,
  code_challenge: challenge, code_challenge_method: 'S256',
}).toString();
// Retain verifier, state and authorizationServer.issuer privately until callback validation.
// Open authorizationURL.href in the user's browser; wait for their consent.
```

The user signs in on Port OS and reviews the requested permissions. Pause for the user; an agent must not approve its own grant, request passwords or manufacture a production sign-in identity. Local functional tests substitute an existing signed fixture identity at this boundary without changing production sign-in.

After approval, the consent page navigates to a one-time Port OS continuation.
That endpoint returns HTTP 302 Found with the exact registered callback in
Location, carrying code, original state and iss. Denial uses the same 302 handoff
with access_denied instead of a code. The authenticated consent fetch returns
200 JSON only for the intermediate continuation; it must be followed by document
navigation, not another fetch. Continuations expire after two minutes and are
single-use. They require no login token and cannot be used to approve consent.

Reject a callback whose state or issuer does not match this attempt. Treat an
error callback as a denied or failed authorization, not a code. Codes and pending
consent expire after ten minutes and are single-use. Do not paste codes,
continuation references or credentials into shared chat or logs. Continue with
[code exchange and token lifecycle](/docs/for-ai/guides/oauth-token-lifecycle.md).

For hosted-client acceptance, preserve the browser network log and approve a
fresh request. Verify the document request to /oauth/authorization-response
returns 302, the next GET reaches the registered client callback, and the client
posts its code and original PKCE verifier to the discovered token endpoint.
Repeat with Deny and verify access_denied without a code. Backend functional and
website browser tests cover these boundaries against an isolated callback;
compatibility with a specific hosted client still requires that live trace.

title: Discover the OAuth server and choose REST or MCP
description: Use this guide to discover the OAuth server for Port OS and choose between the REST API and MCP.
content:
# Discover the OAuth server and choose REST or MCP

This discovery step is shared by every client. The API is https://api.portoperatingsystem.com and the authorization server is https://auth.portoperatingsystem.com. Fetch the API's /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server document anonymously. Read issuer, authorization_endpoint, token_endpoint, registration_endpoint, revocation_endpoint and scopes_supported. Use the returned auth endpoints exactly. The issuer and API resource have different origins; do not use the auth issuer as the API destination or token audience. Port OS exposes OAuth authorization-server metadata here; it does not advertise OpenID Connect discovery or issue OpenID Connect ID tokens.

| Interface | API destination | OAuth resource |
| --- | --- | --- |
| REST | https://api.portoperatingsystem.com plus the documented operation path | https://api.portoperatingsystem.com |
| MCP | https://api.portoperatingsystem.com/mcp, Streamable HTTP | The resource returned by /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp |

An MCP connector can start at https://api.portoperatingsystem.com/mcp and follow its WWW-Authenticate resource_metadata URL. Fetch that public metadata and the authorization server it names. MCP initialization alone does not prove that the account's devices are accessible. Never use a REST token on MCP or an MCP token on REST.

Choose the transport before authorizing. Omitting resource at authorization selects REST. Supply the discovered resource explicitly to select MCP. Code exchange and refresh may omit resource and inherit the grant audience; an explicit resource must stay unchanged. If a REST request fails because you authorized the MCP resource (or the reverse), obtain a new user authorization for the correct resource. Refresh cannot change the token's audience.

Choose one supported [client registration method](/docs/for-ai/guides/oauth-client-registration.md), then follow the same [consent and callback steps](/docs/for-ai/guides/oauth-consent-and-callback.md). If metadata omits registration_endpoint, new DCR registration is unavailable; do not guess a replacement endpoint or silently switch to another client's credentials.

See [scopes and resource rules](/docs/for-ai/guides/authorization-rules.md). Authorization-server scopes_supported describes server vocabulary; a particular client's accepted scopes can be narrower.

## Carry discovery values into every request

This JavaScript fragment initializes a REST connection. Keep `authorizationServer` and `resource` for the consent and token examples; the API base is the protected resource, independently of the discovered auth issuer.

```javascript
const apiBase = 'https://api.portoperatingsystem.com';
const response = await fetch(apiBase + '/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server');
if (!response.ok) throw new Error('OAuth discovery failed');
const authorizationServer = await response.json();
const resource = apiBase;
```

For MCP, assign `resource` from the protected-resource metadata's `resource` field instead. Keep the auth issuer separate from the API resource. A wrong `resource` can produce an `invalid_target` error callback even when client registration succeeded.

title: Set up an OAuth client for Port OS
description: Use this guide when you build an application that needs scoped access to a customer account through OAuth.
content:
# Set up an OAuth client for Port OS

Connect your application with OAuth, ask the user to approve access, and manage its tokens. First [register your client](/docs/for-ai/guides/oauth-client-registration.md). Follow the steps below in order. Use the same REST or MCP resource through the whole connection.

## Discover the OAuth server and choose REST or MCP

This discovery step is shared by every client. The API is https://api.portoperatingsystem.com and the authorization server is https://auth.portoperatingsystem.com. Fetch the API's /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server document anonymously. Read issuer, authorization_endpoint, token_endpoint, registration_endpoint, revocation_endpoint and scopes_supported. Use the returned auth endpoints exactly. The issuer and API resource have different origins; do not use the auth issuer as the API destination or token audience. Port OS exposes OAuth authorization-server metadata here; it does not advertise OpenID Connect discovery or issue OpenID Connect ID tokens.

| Interface | API destination | OAuth resource |
| --- | --- | --- |
| REST | https://api.portoperatingsystem.com plus the documented operation path | https://api.portoperatingsystem.com |
| MCP | https://api.portoperatingsystem.com/mcp, Streamable HTTP | The resource returned by /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp |

An MCP connector can start at https://api.portoperatingsystem.com/mcp and follow its WWW-Authenticate resource_metadata URL. Fetch that public metadata and the authorization server it names. MCP initialization alone does not prove that the account's devices are accessible. Never use a REST token on MCP or an MCP token on REST.

Choose the transport before authorizing. Omitting resource at authorization selects REST. Supply the discovered resource explicitly to select MCP. Code exchange and refresh may omit resource and inherit the grant audience; an explicit resource must stay unchanged. If a REST request fails because you authorized the MCP resource (or the reverse), obtain a new user authorization for the correct resource. Refresh cannot change the token's audience.

Choose one supported [client registration method](/docs/for-ai/guides/oauth-client-registration.md), then follow the same [consent and callback steps](/docs/for-ai/guides/oauth-consent-and-callback.md). If metadata omits registration_endpoint, new DCR registration is unavailable; do not guess a replacement endpoint or silently switch to another client's credentials.

See [scopes and resource rules](/docs/for-ai/guides/authorization-rules.md). Authorization-server scopes_supported describes server vocabulary; a particular client's accepted scopes can be narrower.

### Carry discovery values into every request

This JavaScript fragment initializes a REST connection. Keep `authorizationServer` and `resource` for the consent and token examples; the API base is the protected resource, independently of the discovered auth issuer.

```javascript
const apiBase = 'https://api.portoperatingsystem.com';
const response = await fetch(apiBase + '/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server');
if (!response.ok) throw new Error('OAuth discovery failed');
const authorizationServer = await response.json();
const resource = apiBase;
```

For MCP, assign `resource` from the protected-resource metadata's `resource` field instead. Keep the auth issuer separate from the API resource. A wrong `resource` can produce an `invalid_target` error callback even when client registration succeeded.

Canonical component: [Discover the OAuth server and choose REST or MCP](/docs/for-ai/guides/oauth-discovery.md).

## Obtain user consent and validate the OAuth callback

Use the endpoints and resource from [discovery](/docs/for-ai/guides/oauth-discovery.md) and the client ID and exact callback from [registration](/docs/for-ai/guides/oauth-client-registration.md). These steps are identical for DCR and CIMD, REST and MCP; the chosen resource is the transport-specific input.

`resource` is optional. Omitting it selects the canonical REST audience (the authorization-server issuer). For MCP, supply its discovered `/mcp` resource explicitly. Token exchange and refresh can omit `resource` and inherit the audience bound to the authorization code or refresh token. Explicit mismatches are rejected as `invalid_target`.

1. Start the callback handler the client controls. For a loopback callback, bind its listener locally before opening authorization.
2. Generate a cryptographically random PKCE verifier of 43–128 permitted characters. Compute code_challenge = BASE64URL(SHA256(verifier)), without padding. Generate a separate random state and retain both in this authorization attempt.
3. Open the discovered authorization_endpoint with the following query parameters. Percent-encode parameter values; do not append raw callback URLs or scopes into an unescaped query.

```text
client_id=<registered ID or supported CIMD metadata URL>
redirect_uri=<exact registered callback>
response_type=code
scope=<requested subset of the client's accepted scopes>
resource=<chosen canonical REST or MCP resource>
state=<random client state>
code_challenge=<S256 challenge>
code_challenge_method=S256
```

For REST, use the `resource = authorizationServer.issuer` value retained from discovery. Construct the URL rather than writing an alias into a template. This JavaScript fragment assumes `clientId`, `redirectUri` and `acceptedScope` come from your registration response and callback configuration:

```javascript
const base64url = bytes => btoa(String.fromCharCode(...bytes))
  .replaceAll('+', '-').replaceAll('/', '_').replace(/=+$/, '');
const verifier = base64url(crypto.getRandomValues(new Uint8Array(32)));
const state = base64url(crypto.getRandomValues(new Uint8Array(32)));
const challenge = base64url(new Uint8Array(await crypto.subtle.digest(
  'SHA-256', new TextEncoder().encode(verifier))));
const authorizationURL = new URL(authorizationServer.authorization_endpoint);
authorizationURL.search = new URLSearchParams({
  client_id: clientId, redirect_uri: redirectUri, response_type: 'code',
  scope: acceptedScope, resource, state,
  code_challenge: challenge, code_challenge_method: 'S256',
}).toString();
// Retain verifier, state and authorizationServer.issuer privately until callback validation.
// Open authorizationURL.href in the user's browser; wait for their consent.
```

The user signs in on Port OS and reviews the requested permissions. Pause for the user; an agent must not approve its own grant, request passwords or manufacture a production sign-in identity. Local functional tests substitute an existing signed fixture identity at this boundary without changing production sign-in.

After approval, the consent page navigates to a one-time Port OS continuation.
That endpoint returns HTTP 302 Found with the exact registered callback in
Location, carrying code, original state and iss. Denial uses the same 302 handoff
with access_denied instead of a code. The authenticated consent fetch returns
200 JSON only for the intermediate continuation; it must be followed by document
navigation, not another fetch. Continuations expire after two minutes and are
single-use. They require no login token and cannot be used to approve consent.

Reject a callback whose state or issuer does not match this attempt. Treat an
error callback as a denied or failed authorization, not a code. Codes and pending
consent expire after ten minutes and are single-use. Do not paste codes,
continuation references or credentials into shared chat or logs. Continue with
[code exchange and token lifecycle](/docs/for-ai/guides/oauth-token-lifecycle.md).

For hosted-client acceptance, preserve the browser network log and approve a
fresh request. Verify the document request to /oauth/authorization-response
returns 302, the next GET reaches the registered client callback, and the client
posts its code and original PKCE verifier to the discovered token endpoint.
Repeat with Deny and verify access_denied without a code. Backend functional and
website browser tests cover these boundaries against an isolated callback;
compatibility with a specific hosted client still requires that live trace.

Canonical component: [Obtain user consent and validate the OAuth callback](/docs/for-ai/guides/oauth-consent-and-callback.md).

## Exchange, refresh and revoke scoped OAuth tokens

Complete [callback validation](/docs/for-ai/guides/oauth-consent-and-callback.md) first. For a public DCR/CIMD client, POST application/x-www-form-urlencoded to the discovered token_endpoint with:

```text
grant_type=authorization_code
client_id=<client ID used for authorization>
code=<validated callback code>
redirect_uri=<the same exact callback>
code_verifier=<this attempt's original verifier>
resource=<the same canonical resource used for authorization>
```

Continue with the same discovery values and verifier from the consent example. `code` below must be from a callback whose `state` and `iss` you validated; abort on any callback `error`:

```javascript
const tokenResponse = await fetch(authorizationServer.token_endpoint, {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded' },
  body: new URLSearchParams({
    grant_type: 'authorization_code', client_id: clientId, code,
    redirect_uri: redirectUri, code_verifier: verifier, resource,
  }),
});
if (!tokenResponse.ok) throw new Error('OAuth code exchange failed');
const tokens = await tokenResponse.json(); // Store securely; do not print tokens.
```

Save access_token, refresh_token and returned scope in the connector's secure credential store. Public clients have no client secret. Use Authorization: Bearer <access_token> with REST requests or the MCP HTTP connection, according to that token's resource. A refresh token is never an API credential. [Scopes bound access; resource policies still apply](/docs/for-ai/guides/authorization-rules.md).

Refresh with grant_type=refresh_token, client_id and refresh_token at token_endpoint. The resource parameter is optional for code exchange and refresh: omission inherits the existing grant audience; if supplied, it must match the original resource. Scope may stay the same or narrow; it cannot expand. Credentials rotate: store the newly returned refresh token atomically and stop using the previous one. A revoked or reused refresh token must not be retried in a loop. Reauthorize when the grant no longer permits the intended operation.

Revoke by POSTing application/x-www-form-urlencoded token=<refresh_token>&client_id=<client_id> to revocation_endpoint. Revoked grants stop authorizing both access and refresh requests. Removing a local configuration file alone is not server-side revocation.

Read [the token operation](/docs/for-ai/operations/generateToken.md), [revocation operation](/docs/for-ai/operations/revokeOAuthGrant.md), and [connection recovery](/docs/for-ai/guides/troubleshooting.md) for schemas and failures. Verify account access using [first setup](/docs/for-ai/guides/first-setup.md), then perform only the customer's intended task. Dispatch acceptance is distinct from observed device state.

Canonical component: [Exchange, refresh and revoke scoped OAuth tokens](/docs/for-ai/guides/oauth-token-lifecycle.md).
